resposta:
**Times brasileiros que se classificaram para a Copa Libertadores da América 2021**

Conforme o CONMEBOL e os artigos da Wikipédia, o Brasil teve **7 vagas** (mais uma vaga garantida pelo campeão da Libertadores de 2020). Os clubes brasileiros que avançaram foram:

| Posição / Berto | Clube | Como qualificou‑se |
|---|---|---|
| 1º (campeão da Libertadores 2020) | **Palmeiras** | Campeão da Copa Libertadores 2020 (automático) |
| 2º | **Flamengo** | Campeão do Campeonato Brasileiro 2020 (Série A) |
| 3º | **Internacional** | Vice‑campeão do Campeonato Brasileiro 2020 (Série A) |
| 4º | **Atlético Mineiro** | 3.º colocado no Campeonato Brasileiro 2020 (Série A) |
| 5º | **São Paulo** | 4.º colocado no Campeonato Brasileiro 2020 (Série A) |
| 6º | **Fluminense** | 5.º colocado no Campeonato Brasileiro 2020 (Série A) |
| 7º | **Grêmio** | 6.º colocado no Campeonato Brasileiro 2020 (Série A) – classificou na segunda fase |
| 8º | **Santos** | 8.º colocado no Campeonato Brasileiro 2020 (Série A) – terceiro lugar no Grupo C |

Esses são os clubes brasileiros que entraram na fase de grupos e avançaram até a fase de oitavas de final (round of 16) da Copa Libertadores 2021.  

*Fonte:* Artigo *2021 Copa Libertadores* (Wikipedia – en) e *Copa Libertadores da América de 2021* (pt.wikipedia.org) – tabela “Association | Team (Berth)” e “Group stage”.

A **[Copa Libertadores da América](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_América "Copa Libertadores da América") de [2021](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021 "2021")**, oficialmente **CONMEBOL Libertadores 2021**, foi a 62.ª edição da competição de futebol realizada anualmente pela [Confederação Sul-Americana de Futebol](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederação_Sul-Americana_de_Futebol "Confederação Sul-Americana de Futebol") (CONMEBOL). Participam clubes das dez associações sul-americanas.

Em 13 de maio de 2021, o conselho da CONMEBOL de maneira virtual definiu a cidade de [Montevidéu](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevidéu "Montevidéu"), no Uruguai, como sede das finais da Libertadores e da [Copa Sul-Americana](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Sul-Americana_de_2021 "Copa Sul-Americana de 2021").[[2]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-2) Com isso, o [Estádio Centenario](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Centenario "Estádio Centenario") passou por um processo de modernização pela [CONMEBOL](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederação_Sul-Americana_de_Futebol "Confederação Sul-Americana de Futebol") e contou com a presença de público, já que a maioria da população do Brasil e do Uruguai estava vacinada contra a [COVID-19](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19").[[3]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-3)

O [Palmeiras](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociedade_Esportiva_Palmeiras "Sociedade Esportiva Palmeiras") conquistou seu terceiro título da competição – o segundo seguido, já que conquistou a [Copa Libertadores da América de 2020](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2020 "Copa Libertadores da América de 2020") – ao vencer o [Flamengo](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clube_de_Regatas_do_Flamengo "Clube de Regatas do Flamengo") na [final](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_da_Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2021 "Final da Copa Libertadores da América de 2021") por 2–1.[[4]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-4) Com isso, ganhou o direito de representar a CONMEBOL na [Copa do Mundo de Clubes da FIFA de 2021](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_do_Mundo_de_Clubes_da_FIFA_de_2021 "Copa do Mundo de Clubes da FIFA de 2021"), nos [Emirados Árabes Unidos](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirados_Árabes_Unidos "Emirados Árabes Unidos"), de enfrentar o campeão da [Copa Sul-Americana de 2021](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Sul-Americana_de_2021 "Copa Sul-Americana de 2021") na [Recopa Sul-Americana de 2022](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recopa_Sul-Americana_de_2022 "Recopa Sul-Americana de 2022"), assim como se classificou automaticamente para a fase de grupos da [Copa Libertadores da América de 2022](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2022 "Copa Libertadores da América de 2022"). Ademais, em 14 de março de 2023 a FIFA confirmou a participação do campeão do torneio no [Mundial de Clubes FIFA de 2025](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mundial_de_Clubes_FIFA_de_2025 "Mundial de Clubes FIFA de 2025"), nos Estados Unidos.

## Equipes classificadas

As seguintes 47 equipes das 10 federações filiadas à CONMEBOL se qualificaram para o torneio:

- Campeão da Copa Libertadores da América de 2020
- Campeão da Copa Sul-Americana de 2020
- Brasil: 7 vagas
- Argentina: 6 vagas
- Demais associações: 4 vagas cada

A fase de entrada é determinada da seguinte maneira:

- **Fase de grupos: 28 equipes**
  - Campeão da Copa Libertadores de 2020
  - Campeão da Copa Sul-Americana de 2020
  - Equipes qualificadas para as vagas 1 a 5 da Argentina e do Brasil
  - Equipes qualificadas para as vagas 1 e 2 de todas as outras associações.
- **Segunda fase: 13 equipes**
  - Equipes qualificadas para as vagas 6 e 7 do Brasil
  - Equipe que qualificou para a vaga 6 da Argentina
  - Equipes qualificadas para as vagas 3 e 4 do Chile e Colômbia
  - Equipes qualificadas para a vaga 3 de todas as outras associações.
- **Primeira fase: 6 equipes**
  - Equipes que se qualificaram para a vaga 4 da Bolívia, Equador, Paraguai, Peru, Uruguai e Venezuela

## Sorteio

O sorteio das fases preliminares foi realizado em 5 de fevereiro de 2021, no Centro de Convenções da CONMEBOL em [Luque](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luque_(Paraguai) "Luque (Paraguai)"), no [Paraguai](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguai "Paraguai"). Nesse mesmo dia a primeira fase da [Copa Sul-Americana de 2021](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Sul-Americana_de_2021 "Copa Sul-Americana de 2021") também foi sorteada.[[6]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-7) Para a fase de grupos, um novo sorteio aconteceu em 9 de abril de 2021, onde 32 equipes foram divididas em quatro potes de acordo com a respectiva colocação no [ranking de clubes da CONMEBOL](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranking_de_clubes_da_CONMEBOL "Ranking de clubes da CONMEBOL") e dos classificados das fases preliminares.[[5]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-calendario-5)[[8]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-8)

### Primeira fase

A primeira fase foi disputada por seis equipes provenientes de Bolívia, Equador, Paraguai, Peru, Uruguai e Venezuela, em partidas eliminatórias de ida e volta. Em caso de empate no placar agregado, a [regra do gol fora de casa](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regra_do_gol_fora_de_casa "Regra do gol fora de casa") seria considerada e, persistindo a igualdade, a vaga seria definida na [disputa por pênaltis](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disputa_por_pênaltis "Disputa por pênaltis"). Os confrontos desta fase foram definidos através de sorteio.[[9]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-sorteio2-9)

A terceira fase foi disputada pelas oito equipes vencedoras da fase anterior, em partidas eliminatórias de ida e volta. Em caso de empate no placar agregado, a [regra do gol fora de casa](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regra_do_gol_fora_de_casa "Regra do gol fora de casa") seria considerada e, persistindo a igualdade, a vaga seria definida na [disputa por pênaltis](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disputa_por_pênaltis "Disputa por pênaltis"). Os vencedores de cada confronto se classificam à fase de grupos e os perdedores avançam para a fase de grupos da [Copa Sul-Americana de 2021](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Sul-Americana_de_2021 "Copa Sul-Americana de 2021").[[10]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-10)

## Fase final

Após a conclusão da fase de grupos, um sorteio realizado em 1 de junho definiu o chaveamento das equipes classificadas a partir das oitavas de final até a final.[[12]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-sorteio-12)

As equipes que finalizaram em primeiro lugar na fase de grupos (pote 1 no sorteio) enfrentaram as equipes que finalizaram em segundo lugar (pote 2), podendo ser sorteadas equipes de um mesmo país ou que integraram o mesmo grupo na fase anterior. A pontuação obtida na fase de grupos serve para a definição dos mandos de campo até a semifinal, com as equipes melhores posicionadas sempre realizando o jogo de volta como local (numerados de 1 a 16).[[11]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-regulam-11)[[12]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-sorteio-12)

### Final

Ver artigo principal: [Final da Copa Libertadores da América de 2021](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_da_Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2021 "Final da Copa Libertadores da América de 2021")

O Palmeiras defendeu o título de então campeão e derrotou o Flamengo por 2–1 após a [prorrogação](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prorrogação "Prorrogação"). Após abrir o marcador com gol do meia [Raphael Veiga](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raphael_Veiga "Raphael Veiga") no primeiro tempo, a equipe paulista sofreu o empate no segundo tempo, com gol marcado pelo atacante [Gabriel](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Barbosa "Gabriel Barbosa"), fazendo com que o jogo terminasse no tempo normal em 1–1. Na prorrogação, o atacante [Deyverson](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deyverson "Deyverson") fez o gol do título, após tomar a bola do meia [Andreas Pereira](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Pereira "Andreas Pereira"), levando o Palmeiras ao tricampeonato da competição.[[13]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-13)

- 27 de novembro **[Palmeiras](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociedade_Esportiva_Palmeiras "Sociedade Esportiva Palmeiras") [Brasil](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brasil "Brasil")** **2 – 1 ([pro](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prorrogação "Prorrogação"))** **[Brasil](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brasil "Brasil") [Flamengo](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clube_de_Regatas_do_Flamengo "Clube de Regatas do Flamengo")** [Estádio Centenario](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Centenario "Estádio Centenario"), [Montevidéu](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevidéu "Montevidéu")
- 17:00 ([UTC−3](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC−3 "UTC−3")) [Raphael Veiga](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raphael_Veiga "Raphael Veiga") Gol marcado aos 5 minutos de jogo 5'
 [Deyverson](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deyverson "Deyverson") Gol marcado aos 95 minutos de jogo 95' [Relatório](https://www.conmebol.com/analisis-del-partido?season=2021&competition=420&match=2253364) [Gabriel](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Barbosa "Gabriel Barbosa") Gol marcado aos 72 minutos de jogo 72' **Público:** 45 000[[14]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-público_2021-14)

Valores totais

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Palmeiras_x_Flamengo_-_Libertadores_-_Final_-_Torcida.jpg/250px-Palmeiras_x_Flamengo_-_Libertadores_-_Final_-_Torcida.jpg?utm_source=pt.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ficheiro:Palmeiras_x_Flamengo_-_Libertadores_-_Final_-_Torcida.jpg)Torcida do Palmeiras na arquibancada do Estádio Centenário

Durante a fase de grupos, cada clube recebeu cerca de 1 milhão de [dólares](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dólar "Dólar"), sendo que os dois finalistas arrecadaram aproximadamente 16 milhões de [reais](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_(moeda_brasileira) "Real (moeda brasileira)"). Ao avançar para as oitavas, cada equipe garantiu mais US$ 1,05 milhão. Nas quartas de final, a premiação da Libertadores 2021 foi de US$ 1,5 milhão e, por fim, mais US$ 2 milhões na semifinal. O título do torneio ainda garante mais US$ 15 milhões, enquanto o segundo colocado fica com US$ 6 milhões.[[15]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-premiação-15)

No total, o campeão arrecada pouco mais de R$ 120 milhões, enquanto o segundo colocado fica com cerca de R$ 73 milhões de premiação.[[15]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-premiação-15)

## Notas

- **a.** [**^**](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#ref_Anone) Não definido no momento do sorteio.

- **URU** [**^**](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#ref_URUnone) Como o Campeonato Uruguaio de 2020 ainda estava em disputa com o início da Copa Libertadores de 2021, a [Associação Uruguaia de Futebol](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asociación_Uruguaya_de_Fútbol "Asociación Uruguaya de Fútbol") (AUF) resolveu estabelecer datas de corte para determinar suas equipes classificadas. Conforme essas datas, as vagas foram oferecidas pela AUF após a quinta rodada do Torneio Clausura, na ordem em que as equipes estavam posicionadas na tabela da temporada.[[21]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-21) A primeira data de corte foi em 7 de fevereiro, e a equipe que aceitou a vaga (Liverpool) se classificou como "Uruguai 4" (Nacional, [Montevideo City Torque](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevideo_City_Torque "Montevideo City Torque"), [Peñarol](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Atlético_Peñarol "Club Atlético Peñarol") e [Rentistas](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Atlético_Rentistas "Club Atlético Rentistas") abriram mão). A segunda data foi em 21 de fevereiro, com a equipe que aceitou a vaga (Montevideo Wanderers) se classificando como "Uruguai 3" (Nacional, Montevideo City Torque e Peñarol abriram mão). Caso o campeonato ainda não tivesse sido concluído até 11 de abril, esta seria a última data de corte com as equipes se classificando como "Uruguai 1" e "Uruguai 2".[[22]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-22)

International football competition

The **2021 Copa CONMEBOL Libertadores** was the 62nd edition of the [CONMEBOL Libertadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores "Copa Libertadores") (also referred to as the *Copa Libertadores*), [South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America "South America")'s premier club [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") tournament organized by [CONMEBOL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CONMEBOL "CONMEBOL").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-regulations-1)

Starting from this season, teams must be in the top division of their member association to play in South American club competitions,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-2) except for teams which are champions of the qualifying tournaments or cups.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-3)

On 14 May 2020, CONMEBOL announced the candidate venues for the 2021, 2022 and 2023 club competition finals.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-5) On 13 May 2021, CONMEBOL announced that the [final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores_Final "2021 Copa Libertadores Final") would be played at the [Estadio Centenario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Centenario "Estadio Centenario") in [Montevideo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevideo "Montevideo"), Uruguay on 20 November 2021,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-6) but on 27 July 2021 the final was eventually confirmed to have been rescheduled to 27 November 2021.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-7)

Defending champions [Palmeiras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociedade_Esportiva_Palmeiras "Sociedade Esportiva Palmeiras") won their third Copa Libertadores title after beating fellow Brazilian club [Flamengo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clube_de_Regatas_do_Flamengo "Clube de Regatas do Flamengo") by a 2–1 score after extra time in the final match.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-8) As winners of the 2021 Copa Libertadores, Palmeiras qualified for the [2021 FIFA Club World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_FIFA_Club_World_Cup "2021 FIFA Club World Cup"), and earned the right to play against the winners of the [2021 Copa Sudamericana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Sudamericana "2021 Copa Sudamericana") in the [2022 Recopa Sudamericana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Recopa_Sudamericana "2022 Recopa Sudamericana"). They also automatically qualified for the [2022 Copa Libertadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Copa_Libertadores "2022 Copa Libertadores") group stage.

## Teams

The following 47 teams from the 10 CONMEBOL member associations qualified for the tournament:[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-slots_final-9)

- Copa Libertadores champions
- Copa Sudamericana champions
- Brazil: 7 berths
- Argentina: 6 berths
- All other associations: 4 berths each

The entry stage was determined as follows:[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-slots_final-9)

- Group stage: 28 teams
  - Copa Libertadores champions
  - Copa Sudamericana champions
  - Teams which qualified for berths 1–5 from Argentina and Brazil
  - Teams which qualified for berths 1–2 from all other associations
- Second stage: 13 teams
  - Teams which qualified for berths 6–7 from Brazil
  - Team which qualified for berth 6 from Argentina
  - Teams which qualified for berths 3–4 from Chile and Colombia
  - Teams which qualified for berth 3 from all other associations
- First stage: 6 teams
  - Teams which qualified for berth 4 from Bolivia, Ecuador, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay and Venezuela

1.  
  **Argentina (ARG):**
  - On 28 April 2020, the [Argentine Football Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentine_Football_Association "Argentine Football Association") announced the abandonment of the [2020 Copa de la Superliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Copa_de_la_Superliga "2020 Copa de la Superliga") and the culmination of the 2019–20 season due to the [COVID-19 pandemic in Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Argentina "COVID-19 pandemic in Argentina"). The six Argentina berths of the 2021 Copa Libertadores were awarded to the following:[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-13)
    - The *Argentina 1* berth was awarded to the [2019–20 Superliga Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019–20_Argentine_Primera_División "2019–20 Argentine Primera División") champions.
    - The *Argentina 2* berth, originally awarded to the 2020 Copa de la Superliga champions, was awarded to the winner of a tournament to be played in the second semester of 2020, later confirmed to be the [2020 Copa de la Liga Profesional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Copa_de_la_Liga_Profesional "2020 Copa de la Liga Profesional").
    - The *Argentina 3* berth was awarded to the [2019–20 Copa Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019–20_Copa_Argentina "2019–20 Copa Argentina") champions, provided that government directives allowed for it to be concluded.
    - The *Argentina 4*, *Argentina 5*, and *Argentina 6* berths were awarded to the three best teams of the [2019–20 Superliga Argentina and 2020 Copa de la Superliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019–20_Argentine_Primera_División#International_qualification "2019–20 Argentine Primera División") aggregate table at the time of the suspension of the latter competition not yet qualified.
  - On 11 December 2020 it was confirmed that the 2019–20 Copa Argentina would not be completed in time to award its winner a berth into the 2021 Copa Libertadores, therefore the *Argentina 3* berth was reallocated to the best team of the 2019–20 Superliga Argentina and 2020 Copa de la Superliga aggregate table not yet qualified.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-14)

2.  
  **Bolivia (BOL):** The 2020 Clausura tournament was not held due to the [COVID-19 pandemic in Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Bolivia "COVID-19 pandemic in Bolivia"), therefore the *Bolivia 2*, *Bolivia 3*, and *Bolivia 4* berths of the 2021 Copa Libertadores were reallocated to the [2020 Apertura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Bolivian_Primera_División_season#Torneo_Apertura "2020 Bolivian Primera División season") runners-up, third and fourth-placed teams, respectively.

3.  
  **Chile (CHI):** On 30 December 2020, the Council of Presidents of the [ANFP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asociación_Nacional_de_Fútbol_Profesional "Asociación Nacional de Fútbol Profesional") decided that the *Chile 4* berth, originally awarded to the [2020 Copa Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Copa_Chile?action=edit&redlink=1 "2020 Copa Chile (page does not exist)") champions, would be awarded to the fourth-placed team of the [2020 Chilean Primera División](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Chilean_Primera_División "2020 Chilean Primera División"), given that the 2020 Copa Chile would not be held before the start of the 2021 Copa Libertadores.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-15)

4.  
  **Colombia (COL):**
  - On 25 July 2020, [DIMAYOR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/División_Mayor_del_Fútbol_Profesional_Colombiano "División Mayor del Fútbol Profesional Colombiano") decided that the [2020 Categoría Primera A season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Categoría_Primera_A_season "2020 Categoría Primera A season"), suspended from 13 March due to the [COVID-19 pandemic in Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Colombia "COVID-19 pandemic in Colombia"), would only have a single tournament played for the remainder of the season. Therefore, the *Colombia 1* berth of the 2021 Copa Libertadores, originally awarded to the 2020 Apertura champions, and the *Colombia 2* berth, originally awarded to the 2020 Finalización champions, would instead be awarded to the champions and runners-up of that single tournament, respectively.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-16)
  - On 9 September 2020, DIMAYOR confirmed the reallocation of the four Colombia berths of the 2021 Copa Libertadores as follows:[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-17)
    - The *Colombia 1* berth was awarded to the 2020 Primera A champions.
    - The *Colombia 2* berth was awarded to the 2020 Primera A runners-up.
    - The *Colombia 3* berth was awarded to the [2020 Primera A aggregate table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Categoría_Primera_A_season#Aggregate_table "2020 Categoría Primera A season") best team not yet qualified.
    - The *Colombia 4* berth, originally awarded to the [2020 Copa Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Copa_Colombia "2020 Copa Colombia") champions, was awarded to the 2020 Primera A aggregate table 2nd best team not yet qualified.

5.  
  **Uruguay (URU):** Given that the [2020 Primera División](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Uruguayan_Primera_División_season "2020 Uruguayan Primera División season") was not concluded before the start of the [2021 Copa Libertadores qualifying stages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores_qualifying_stages "2021 Copa Libertadores qualifying stages") due to the [COVID-19 pandemic in Uruguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Uruguay "COVID-19 pandemic in Uruguay"), on 14 January 2021 the League Council of the [Uruguayan Football Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uruguayan_Football_Association "Uruguayan Football Association") approved a temporary modification to the qualification method of Uruguayan teams. Since associations had to formally inform CONMEBOL of the teams that would take part in international competition ahead of the start of competition, some international berths were decided based on deadlines set according to the dates the respective Copa Libertadores rounds were scheduled for as well as the placements of teams in the [2020 Primera División](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Uruguayan_Primera_División_season#Aggregate_table "2020 Uruguayan Primera División season") aggregate table at the time of those deadlines:[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-18)
  - The *Uruguay 4* berth was awarded to the best eligible team of the 2020 Primera División aggregate table as of 7 February 2021, considering that the Copa Libertadores first stage was scheduled to begin on 23 February 2021. [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_F.C._(Montevideo) "Liverpool F.C. (Montevideo)") ([2020 Primera División](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Uruguayan_Primera_División_season#Aggregate_table "2020 Uruguayan Primera División season") aggregate table fifth place as of 7 February 2021) accepted the berth after the top four of the aggregate table at that moment ([Nacional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Nacional_de_Football "Club Nacional de Football"), [Montevideo City Torque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevideo_City_Torque "Montevideo City Torque"), [Peñarol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peñarol "Peñarol"), and [Rentistas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C.A._Rentistas "C.A. Rentistas")) all declined to take the berth.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-19)
  - The *Uruguay 3* berth was awarded to the best eligible team of the 2020 Primera División aggregate table as of 21 February 2021, considering that the Copa Libertadores second stage was scheduled to begin on 9 March 2021. [Montevideo Wanderers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevideo_Wanderers_F.C. "Montevideo Wanderers F.C.") (2020 Primera División aggregate table fifth place as of 21 February 2021) accepted the berth after the top three of the aggregate table at that moment (Nacional, Montevideo City Torque, and Peñarol) all declined to take the berth, and fourth-placed Liverpool was already qualified as *Uruguay 4*.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-20)
  - Teams were offered the chance to accept or decline the berths they were eligible for at the time of the respective deadlines.

6.  
  **Venezuela (VEN):** On 15 May 2020, the [Venezuelan Football Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venezuelan_Football_Federation "Venezuelan Football Federation") decided the permanent suspension of the [2020 Venezuelan Primera División season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Venezuelan_Primera_División_season "2020 Venezuelan Primera División season") and the voiding of the standings and results recorded due to the [COVID-19 pandemic in Venezuela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Venezuela "COVID-19 pandemic in Venezuela").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-22) The allocation of the four Venezuela berths of the 2021 Copa Libertadores would be announced at a later time, with the FVF confirming a will to organize a new tournament in which sporting merit, club licensing requirements, and medical protocols were applied.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-23) The definitive berth allocations were confirmed by the FVF on 18 September 2020.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-24)

The draw for the qualifying stages was held on 5 February 2021, 12:00 [PYST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_in_Paraguay "Time in Paraguay") ([UTC−3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC−03:00 "UTC−03:00")), at the CONMEBOL Convention Centre in [Luque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luque "Luque"), [Paraguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguay "Paraguay").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-Qualifying_stages_draw-28)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-fixture_1S-2S-31)

Teams were seeded by their *CONMEBOL Clubs ranking* as of 1 February 2021 (shown in parentheses),[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-ranking-33) taking into account the following three factors:[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-34)

1. Performance in the last 10 years, taking into account Copa Libertadores and Copa Sudamericana results in the period 2011–2020.
2. Historical coefficient, taking into account Copa Libertadores and Copa Sudamericana results in the period 1960–2010 and 2002-2010 respectively.
3. Local tournament champion, with bonus points awarded to domestic league champions of the last 10 years

For the first stage, the six teams were drawn into three ties (E1–E3), with the teams from Pot 1 hosting the second leg.

- Second stage winner C1 vs. Second stage winner C8
- Second stage winner C2 vs. Second stage winner C7
- Second stage winner C3 vs. Second stage winner C6
- Second stage winner C4 vs. Second stage winner C5

Teams from the same association could not be drawn into the same group, excluding the four winners of the third stage, which were seeded in Pot 4 and whose identity was not known at the time of the draw, and could be drawn into the same group with another team from the same association.

The draw for the round of 16 was held on 1 June 2021, 12:00 [PYT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_in_Paraguay "Time in Paraguay") ([UTC−4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC−04:00 "UTC−04:00")), at the CONMEBOL Convention Center in [Luque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luque "Luque"), [Paraguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguay "Paraguay").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-Final_stages_draw-30) For the round of 16, the 16 teams were drawn into eight ties (A–H) between a group winner (Pot 1) and a group runner-up (Pot 2), with the group winners hosting the second leg. Teams from the same association or the same group could be drawn into the same tie (Regulations Article 2.2.3.2).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-regulations-1)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-36)

## Qualifying stages

Main article: [2021 Copa Libertadores qualifying stages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores_qualifying_stages "2021 Copa Libertadores qualifying stages")

In the qualifying stages, each tie was played on a home-and-away [two-legged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-legged_tie "Two-legged tie") basis. If tied on aggregate, the [away goals rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Away_goals_rule "Away goals rule") was used. If still tied, [extra time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overtime_(sports)#Association_football "Overtime (sports)") was not played, and a [penalty shoot-out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penalty_shoot-out_(association_football) "Penalty shoot-out (association football)") was used to determine the winner (Regulations Article 2.4.3).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-regulations-1) The qualifying stages were structured as follows:

- **First stage (6 teams):** The three winners of the first stage advanced to the second stage to join the 13 teams which were given byes to the second stage.
- **Second stage (16 teams):** The eight winners of the second stage advanced to the third stage.
- **Third stage (8 teams):** The four winners of the third stage advanced to the [group stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores_group_stage "2021 Copa Libertadores group stage") to join the 28 direct entrants. The four teams eliminated in the third stage entered the [Copa Sudamericana group stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Sudamericana_group_stage "2021 Copa Sudamericana group stage").

## Group stage

Main article: [2021 Copa Libertadores group stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores_group_stage "2021 Copa Libertadores group stage")

In the group stage, each group is played on a home-and-away [round-robin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round-robin_tournament "Round-robin tournament") basis. The teams are ranked according to the following criteria: 1. [Points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Points_(association_football) "Points (association football)") (3 points for a win, 1 point for a draw, and 0 points for a loss); 2. [Goal difference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goal_difference "Goal difference"); 3. Goals scored; 4. Away goals scored; 5. CONMEBOL ranking (Regulations Article 2.4.2).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-regulations-1)

The winners and runners-up of each group advanced to the [round of 16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores_final_stages#Round_of_16 "2021 Copa Libertadores final stages") of the [final stages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores_final_stages "2021 Copa Libertadores final stages"). The third-placed teams of each group entered the [round of 16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Sudamericana_final_stages#Round_of_16 "2021 Copa Sudamericana final stages") of the [2021 Copa Sudamericana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Sudamericana "2021 Copa Sudamericana").

## Final stages

Main article: [2021 Copa Libertadores final stages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores_final_stages "2021 Copa Libertadores final stages")

Starting from the round of 16, the teams played a [single-elimination tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-elimination_tournament "Single-elimination tournament") with the following rules:[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-regulations-1)

- In the round of 16, quarter-finals and semi-finals, each tie was played on a home-and-away [two-legged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-legged_tie "Two-legged tie") basis, with the higher-seeded team hosting the second leg (Regulations Article 2.2.3.2). If tied on aggregate, the [away goals rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Away_goals_rule "Away goals rule") was used. If still tied, [extra time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overtime_(sports)#Association_football "Overtime (sports)") was not played, and a [penalty shoot-out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penalty_shoot-out_(association_football) "Penalty shoot-out (association football)") was used to determine the winners (Regulations Article 2.4.3).
- The final was played as a single match at a venue pre-selected by CONMEBOL, with the higher-seeded team designated as the "home" team for administrative purposes (Regulations Article 2.2.3.5). If tied after regulation, 30 minutes of extra time were played. If still tied after extra time, a penalty shoot-out was used to determine the winners (Regulations Article 2.4.4).

# Cabrita: closing the gap for foreign languages

Marcos Piau Paulo Finardi Pedro Gengo Piero Esposito Vinicius Caridá

email: {celiolarcher, marcos.piau.vieira, pfinardi, pedro.gengo.lourenco, piero.skywalker, vfcarida}@gmail.com  

###### Abstract

The strategy of training the model from scratch in a specific language or domain serves two essential purposes: i) enhancing performance in the particular linguistic or domain context, and ii) ensuring effective tokenization. The main limitation inherent to this approach lies in the associated cost, which can reach six to seven-digit dollar values, depending on the model size and the number of parameters involved.

The main solution to overcome the cost challenge is to rely on available pre-trained models, which, despite recent advancements such as the LLaMA and LLaMA-2 models, still demonstrate inefficiency for certain specific domain problems or prove ineffective in scenarios involving conversational memory resources, given the large number of tokens required to represent text.

To overcome this issue, we present a methodology named Cabrita, which, as our research demonstrates, successfully addresses the performance and efficient tokenization problem, all at an affordable cost. We believe that this methodology can be applied to any transformer-like architecture model. To validate the study, we conducted continuous pre-training exclusively using Portuguese text on a 3-billion-parameter model known as OpenLLaMA, resulting in a model named openCabrita 3B. The openCabrita 3B also features a new tokenizer that results in a significant reduction in the number of tokens required to represent the text. In our assessment, for few-shot learning tasks, we achieved similar results with this 3B model compared to a traditional continuous pre-training approach as well as to 7B models English pre-trained models.

## 1 Introduction

While the Portuguese language does not suffer from a lack of data for training transformer-based language models, a native speaker can readily perceive limitations in text generation and performance of pre-trained models predominantly based on English language data. Following the research conducted in Sabiá [[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib1 "")], we share the perspective that the conventional practice of simultaneously pre-training models in multiple languages fails to capture the cultural richness and intrinsic knowledge of each language.

As demonstrated in the study [[2](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib2 "")], language-specific adapted tokenizers have the potential to significantly enhance the monolingual performance of multilingual models.

Considering that pre-training a model in a single language with a specific tokenizer leads to notably superior performance, it’s natural to question why there aren’t more language-specific models. However, the answer lies in a crucial factor: cost. An example of this is the cost of the LLaMa 2 7B model, which required a total of 184,320 hours of processing on GPU A-100 80-GB. Assuming a conservative estimate that 1 hour of this GPU costs $1, the resulting cost approaches $200,000 significantly. This underscores how the substantial investments required to create and maintain language-specific language models can pose a significant financial challenge.

This article investigates an alternative approach to zero-shot pre-training based on three fundamental principles: low cost, performance optimization, and efficient tokenization. This approach aims to enable the model to use fewer tokens and minimize inference time compared to existing multilingual models.

## 2 Methodology

### 2.1 LLaMA Models

The LLaMA models are Large Language Models developed by the Meta AI’s team [[3](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib3 "")]. Based on the well-established transformers architecture it incorporates several novel training and inference mechanisms, notably the use of Pre-normalization [[4](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib4 "")], the SwiGlu activation function [[5](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib5 "")] and the inclusion of Rotary Embeddings [[6](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib6 "")].

The primary distinction of LLaMA models lies in the magnitude of pre-training data utilized during their development, scaling from the standard 300 billion tokens in the optimal Chinchila’s law pattern [[7](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib7 "")] to an extensive 1 trillion tokens. Although this setup incurs increased resource costs during training, it significantly improves the state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance for all model sizes at the time of release. As a result, inference costs are reduced, as smaller models can achieve comparable levels of performance, thereby justifying the theoretical non-optimal behavior during pre-training.

After its introduction, several other Large Language Models have been trained following a similar approach, facilitating further advancements in SOTA standards, particularly for smaller models. For this study, we adopt the OpenLLaMA implementation[[8](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib8 "")], an open-source Apache 2.0 alternative with the same recipe as the open-science-only LLaMA.

### 2.2 openCabrita Models

Despite the proliferation of numerous open source Large Language Models in recent years, the availability of generative models for non-English languages remains a persistent problem.

While employing English models for other languages might seem feasible, their performance typically falls short of optimal, even when utilizing multilingual options or implementing Instruction Fine Tuning [[9](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib9 "")] in the target language [[10](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib10 ""), [11](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib11 ""), [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib1 "")].

Taking this aspect into consideration, this work introduces the openCabrita models, a collection of checkpoints derived from the OpenLLama models. These models undergo additional pre-training using a Portuguese corpus, inspired by the methodology proposed in [[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib1 "")], while also incorporating additional tokenizer adaption.
The training procedure will be elaborated on in the next subsections.

#### 2.2.1 Tokenizer adaptation

One of the main challenges of adapting a Large Language Model to a new language that is underrepresented in its pre-training is the tokenizer behavior.
This is the case for the Portuguese language in the OpenLLaMA model, where despite the 1 trillion tokens used, just a small part were non-English.
The default tokenizer, in such cases, tends to be overly verbose for non-English examples, necessitating the division of the text into too small parts.

This behavior is undesirable for two primary reasons: i) it shatters the amount of information contained within each sub-unit processed by the model, potentially making it more challenging to understand long-term relations within the context; and ii) it escalates the computational cost of both training and inference, as it increases the number of tokens that need to be processed for the same text sample.

However, the inclusion of a new tokenizer in a pre-trained model poses a challenge, as there exists a direct mapping between the tokens used in pre-training and the model’s embedding representation. Merely replacing the tokenizer would break this mapping, likely resulting in odd model behavior and potentially requiring a considerable amount of additional pre-training to learn the new association pattern.

To address this issue, the approach taken in this work involves adapting the tokenizer to the new language while preserving the knowledge of the original language already embedded in the model. Inspired by the work of [[11](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib11 "")], this process involved three steps:

- •     Training a new tokenizer exclusively on Portuguese data sourced from Wikipedia. SentencePiece [[12](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib12 "")] implementation was used for this purpose, resulting in a tokenizer with 40,000 tokens.

- •     Merging the original tokenizer with the newly created Portuguese tokenizer. During this merging process, all tokens present in the original tokenizer were retained, and the new Portuguese tokens that were not yet represented in the vocabulary were appended until a total of 52,000 tokens were reached. The precedence level of each merge – BPE Score in the SentencePiece implementation – was maintained from both tokenizers, given that this led to a better token compression level.

- •     Resizing the model’s embedding and head matrix to accommodate the newly added tokens. The new rows corresponding to the Portuguese tokens were appended to the end of the original matrix to ensure that the existing token mapping remained unaffected.

The result was a bilingual tokenizer, able to handle both English and Portuguese content efficiently.

#### 2.2.2 Continuous pre-training

We use the Portuguese subset of the mC4 dataset [[13](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib13 "")] (hereafter called mC4-pt) as our pretraining corpus. Following the recipe in [[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib1 "")], we also apply quality filters based on MassiveText [[14](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib14 "")] to ensure our model is trained using high-quality documents.

First, we normalize each document independently using ftfy [[15](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib15 "")]. Then, we apply the quality filters. Unlike MassiveText, which only considers the stop words {the, be, to, of, and, that, have, with}, we use the Portuguese stop words from nltk [[16](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib16 "")]; we also keep only documents with at least 200 unique tokens, following the the procedure outlined in [[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib1 "")]. A document is kept in the dataset if it does not fall into any of the quality filters. Table [7](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#A2.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Appendix B mC4-pt cleaning filters ‣ Cabrita: closing the gap for foreign languages") shows the contribution of each filter to the final filtered dataset.

To estimate the total number of training tokens without processing the entire dataset, we assume that the remaining shards have similar sizes and behavior with respect to the quality filters. Based on this estimation, the unfiltered mC4-pt training dataset consists of approximately 169 million documents and 188 billion tokens, which reduces to 133 million documents and 170 billion tokens after applying the low-quality filters. To convert these documents into training examples, we add <|bos|> and <|eos|> tokens to each document, and then pack these documents into sequences of 2048 tokens.

We perform the continuous pre-training step on TPUs using the EasyLM, which is a framework built in JAX/Flax and is a one-stop solution for training LLMs on TPU and GPU devices.

To perform continued pre-training in the Portuguese language, the original script and hyper-parameters of OpenLLaMA training were employed. The model was initialized with the OpenLLaMA weights and then trained on an additional 7 billion tokens extracted from the Portuguese dataset.

The learning objective was the standard causal language modeling loss with the learning rate set to increase linearly from 0 to 3e-4 over 2,000 steps, followed by a cosine decrease to 3e-5 for the remaining 248,000 steps. The optimization algorithm used was AdamW, with a weight decay of 0.1, <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\beta_{1}" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p6.m1"><semantics><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> --> β1\beta_{1} set to 0.9, <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="\beta_{2}" id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p6.m2"><semantics><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> --> β2\beta_{2} set to 0.99, and a gradient clip value of 1.0.

For training, a TPU v3-8 was utilized, with batches of 16, each containing a sequence of 2048 tokens. To achieve the target of 2048 samples in a batch, 128 accumulation steps were performed. This configuration resulted in a throughput of 7,900 tokens/second for the 3B model.

## 3 Evaluation

### 3.1 Tokenizer efficiency

For evaluating how alterations to the tokenizer affect text representation, a set of experiments were performed. These experiments involved the comparison of various tokenizer alternatives coming from different models and trained on distinct corpora. Figure [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3.1 Tokenizer efficiency ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ Cabrita: closing the gap for foreign languages") presents a comparison of the token count required to represent 7400 words of the Constitutional law of the USA in both English and Portuguese (translated) for each of these tokenizer variations.

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1/pics/tokenization_junto.png)Figure 1: Tokenizer efficiency: the X axis show the number of tokens required to represent 7400 words of the Constitutional law of the USA in English, while the Y axis shows the same, but using a Portuguese translated version. The size of each sphere represents the vocabulary size of each tokenizer.

It can be noted that the standard OpenLLaMA implementation demonstrates highly inefficient behavior when applied to Portuguese data. It necessitates over 50% more tokens for representing the same text, in contrast to the multilingual Bloom and Portuguese pre-trained models (e.g. BERTimbau [[17](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib17 "")], PTT5 [[18](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib18 "")], Bertaú [[19](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib19 "")]). While certain other LLaMA-based implementations exhibit improved token counts, such as MPT [[20](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib20 "")] and Falcon [[21](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib21 "")], some inefficiency remains. This observation holds true even in comparison with chatGPT [[22](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib22 "")], which possesses a larger vocabulary than these LLaMA implementations.

In contrast to these choices, the Cabrita tokenizer demonstrated the ability to enhance the OpenLLaMA token requirements. It achieved a reduction of over 35% in the token requirements, bringing it in line with the token counts of the Bloom and native Portuguese implementations.

Furthermore, upon examining the token count in English, the Cabrita tokenizer even exhibited a slight improvement in the token count when compared with the original OpenLLaMA tokenizer, with no indication of degradation in this regard.

Ultimately, the Cabrita approach presents an excellent trade-off between Portuguese and English considerations, especially when seeking models with comparable vocabulary sizes (52.000 tokens for Cabrita versus 250.680 tokens for Bloom).

### 3.2 Portuguese Benchmark results

To assess the efficacy of this proposal, 8 Portuguese evaluation datasets were employed across a variety of tasks: ASSIN 2 RTE and STS [[23](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib23 "")], FaQuAD [[24](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib24 "")], TweetSentBr [[25](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib25 "")] are inherently in Portuguese, while for AG News [[26](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib26 "")], IMDB [[27](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib27 "")], SST2 [[28](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib28 "")] and BoolQ [[29](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib29 "")] translated versions provided by the authors of the Sabiá series paper were utilized.
Poeta’s benchmark [[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib1 "")] was not executed in our study due to the unavailability of its implementation at the time of our publication.

Table [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.2 Portuguese Benchmark results ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ Cabrita: closing the gap for foreign languages") provides an overview of the datasets along with the specific few-shot configuration employed in each experiment.

Table 1: Number of few-show samples and main metric for each task

A diverse array of tasks was carefully selected, spanning from binary and multi-class classification to Extractive Question Answering (QA). However, the absence of a comprehensive Portuguese benchmark prevented the utilization of a more extensive task set.

The Table [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.2 Portuguese Benchmark results ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ Cabrita: closing the gap for foreign languages") exhibits the performance comparison of openCabrita3B with the base openLLaMA3B and a subsequent pre-training version that employs the openLLaMA tokenizer (referred to as openCabrita3BPTOnly).

Table 2: This Table shows the results obtained for each task and each model. The configurations are the ones presented in the Table [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.2 Portuguese Benchmark results ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ Cabrita: closing the gap for foreign languages").

The results are mixed but somewhat favoring openCabrita3B. When openCabrita3B performs better, it is notably superior, as in ASSIN 2 RTE, TweetSentBr, and IMDB tasks. When openCabrita3BPTOnly outperforms, openCabrita3B is usually close, just a few scores behind. While ASSIN 2 STS is the only task where the original openLLaMA3b shows a better performance, which is unexpected but consistent with what was observed in other experiments [[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib1 "")].

Nevertheless, it is evident that the Cabrita approach, which involves adapting the tokenizer, can offer at least a comparable performance level in contrast to the conventional continued pre-training. This equivalent performance improvement also comes with the added benefit of enhanced inference efficiency.

Table [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#S3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 3.2 Portuguese Benchmark results ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ Cabrita: closing the gap for foreign languages") shows the same set of tasks, with a focus on comparing the performance of openCabrita3B to the outcomes presented in the Sabiá paper. It’s important to highlight that while the datasets remain the same, possible variations in the execution scripts require a cautious approach when drawing comparisons.

Table 3: This Table shows the results obtained for each task and each model for Portuguese datasets. The configurations are presented in Table [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.2 Portuguese Benchmark results ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ Cabrita: closing the gap for foreign languages"). The * symbol represents results that come from a different running script than ours, so the results need to be compared carefully.

The performance of openCabrita3B seems very satisfactory for a model of its size. It consistently outperforms GPT-J, a model with 6B parameters, and demonstrates competitiveness with LLaMA-7B. In the case of continued pre-training versions of these models, openCabrita3B closely approaches the performance of Sabiá-J, while slightly lagging behind Sabiá-7B.

These results do not cast any negative light on openCabrita3B, as it performs admirably despite having only half the parameter size compared to the other four options.

### 3.3 English Benchmark results

To assess the efficacy of this approach and demonstrate its bilingual capabilities, we conducted a series of evaluations using diverse English datasets, ensuring a comprehensive understanding of its performance. Table [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#S3.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 3.3 English Benchmark results ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ Cabrita: closing the gap for foreign languages") presents the performance of openCabrita in comparison with models trained mainly in English and without any fine-tuning for a specific language.

Despite a slight decrease in performance for English, the model’s capabilities remained robust and competitive across languages. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of different tokenizers—Open Llama and Cabrita—on the model’s output. Encouragingly, both tokenizers yielded highly consistent results, indicating that the introduction of new tokens had minimal impact on the model’s overall performance. This observation highlights the model’s resilience and suggests its versatility for diverse applications without significant trade-offs in performance.

Table 4: This Table shows the results obtained for each task and each model for English datasets. The * symbol represents results that come from a different running script than ours, so the results need to be compared carefully.

## 4 Conclusion and next steps

This work is currently in progress and requires further development in terms of a more comprehensive set of models and experiments before arriving at any definitive conclusions. However, the outcomes obtained from modifying the tokenizer prior to performing continuous pre-training seem very promising.

Even in the absence of state-of-the-art performance enhancements, the openCabrita3b reaches a comparable metrics level when compared to the standard continuous pre-training approach while also improving inference time — an imperative factor in the context of deploying models for such applications that is commonly overlooked.

Looking ahead, the authors have outlined the following as their forthcoming initiatives:

- •     Test the same strategy in a more diverse set of base models

- •     Establish some type of benchmark and reperform runs for other models in order to have a comparison with the same running methodology

## 5 Limitations

Scaling beyond 3B and for other languages Despite our best efforts, certain ranges of model sizes and experiments remain beyond our reach due to budget constraints. Consequently, our experimentation was limited to the Portuguese language and 3B size models.

But, since the good results obtained, we are firmly convinced that employing larger-scale models could yield results at least as promising. This line of thinking could similarly be applied to other foreign languages, particularly considering the successful experiment with Chinese presented in [[11](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib11 "")].

Comparison to other base models and adapting strategies Due to the absence of a structured benchmark like Harness [[30](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.11878v1#bib.bib30 "")] for the Portuguese language, our capacity to compare with other models and strategies for the same tasks is confined to the experiments we are able to perform. Consequently, the scope of comparisons we can undertake in this paper is restricted, both in terms of quantity and depth.

We thank Google Cloud for the TPU grant through the TRC program.

CABRITA: CLOSING THE GAP FOR FOREIGN LANGUAGES

PREPRINT

Celio Larcher

Marcos Piau

Paulo Finardi

Pedro Gengo

Piero Esposito

Vinicius Caridá

22h, Brazil

email:

{celiolarcher, marcos.piau.vieira, pfinardi, pedro.gengo.lourenco,

piero.skywalker, vfcarida}@gmail.com

ABSTRACT

The strategy of training the model from scratch in a specific language or domain serves two essential  
purposes: i) enhancing performance in the particular linguistic or domain context, and ii) ensuring  
effective tokenization. The main limitation inherent to this approach lies in the associated cost,  
which can reach six to seven-digit dollar values, depending on the model size and the number of  
parameters involved.

The main solution to overcome the cost challenge is to rely on available pre-trained models, which,  
despite recent advancements such as the LLaMA and LLaMA-2 models, still demonstrate ineffi-  
ciency for certain specific domain problems or prove ineffective in scenarios involving conversa-  
tional memory resources, given the large number of tokens required to represent text.

To overcome this issue, we present a methodology named Cabrita, which, as our research demon-  
strates, successfully addresses the performance and efficient tokenization problem, all at an afford-  
able cost. We believe that this methodology can be applied to any transformer-like architecture  
model. To validate the study, we conducted continuous pre-training exclusively using Portuguese  
text on a 3-billion-parameter model known as OpenLLaMA, resulting in a model named openCabrita  
3B. The openCabrita 3B also features a new tokenizer that results in a significant reduction in the  
number of tokens required to represent the text. In our assessment, for few-shot learning tasks,  
we achieved similar results with this 3B model compared to a traditional continuous pre-training  
approach as well as to 7B models English pre-trained models.

1

Introduction

While the Portuguese language does not suffer from a lack of data for training transformer-based language models, a  
native speaker can readily perceive limitations in text generation and performance of pre-trained models predominantly  
based on English language data. Following the research conducted in Sabiá [\[1\], ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#7)we share the perspective that the  
conventional practice of simultaneously pre-training models in multiple languages fails to capture the cultural richness  
and intrinsic knowledge of each language.

As demonstrated in the study [\[2\], ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#7)language-specific adapted tokenizers have the potential to significantly enhance the  
monolingual performance of multilingual models.

Considering that pre-training a model in a single language with a specific tokenizer leads to notably superior perfor-  
mance, it’s natural to question why there aren’t more language-specific models. However, the answer lies in a crucial  
factor: cost. An example of this is the cost of the LLaMa 2 7B model, which required a total of 184,320 hours of pro-  
cessing on GPU A-100 80-GB. Assuming a conservative estimate that 1 hour of this GPU costs $1, the resulting cost  
approaches $200,000 significantly. This underscores how the substantial investments required to create and maintain  
language-specific language models can pose a significant financial challenge.

Cabrita: closing the gap for foreign languages

PREPRINT

This article investigates an alternative approach to zero-shot pre-training based on three fundamental principles: low  
cost, performance optimization, and efficient tokenization. This approach aims to enable the model to use fewer tokens  
and minimize inference time compared to existing multilingual models.

2

Methodology

2.1

LLaMA Models

The LLaMA models are Large Language Models developed by the Meta AI’s team [\[3\]. ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#7)Based on the well-established  
transformers architecture it incorporates several novel training and inference mechanisms, notably the use of Pre-  
normalization [\[4\], ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#7)the SwiGlu activation function [\[5\] ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#7)and the inclusion of Rotary Embeddings [\[6\].](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#7)

The primary distinction of LLaMA models lies in the magnitude of pre-training data utilized during their development,  
scaling from the standard 300 billion tokens in the optimal Chinchila’s law pattern [\[7\] ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#7)to an extensive 1 trillion to-  
kens. Although this setup incurs increased resource costs during training, it significantly improves the state-of-the-art  
(SOTA) performance for all model sizes at the time of release. As a result, inference costs are reduced, as smaller  
models can achieve comparable levels of performance, thereby justifying the theoretical non-optimal behavior during  
pre-training.

After its introduction, several other Large Language Models have been trained following a similar approach, facili-  
tating further advancements in SOTA standards, particularly for smaller models. For this study, we adopt the Open-  
LLaMA implementation [\[8\], ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#7)an open-source Apache 2.0 alternative with the same recipe as the open-science-only  
LLaMA.

2.2

openCabrita Models

Despite the proliferation of numerous open source Large Language Models in recent years, the availability of genera-  
tive models for non-English languages remains a persistent problem.

While employing English models for other languages might seem feasible, their performance typically falls short of  
optimal, even when utilizing multilingual options or implementing Instruction Fine Tuning [\[9\] ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#7)in the target language  
[\[1, 10, 11\].](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#7)

Taking this aspect into consideration, this work introduces the openCabrita models, a collection of checkpoints derived  
from the OpenLLama models. These models undergo additional pre-training using a Portuguese corpus, inspired by  
the methodology proposed in [\[1\], ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#7)while also incorporating additional tokenizer adaption. The training procedure will  
be elaborated on in the next subsections.

2.2.1

Tokenizer adaptation

One of the main challenges of adapting a Large Language Model to a new language that is underrepresented in its  
pre-training is the tokenizer behavior. This is the case for the Portuguese language in the OpenLLaMA model, where  
despite the 1 trillion tokens used, just a small part were non-English. The default tokenizer, in such cases, tends to be  
overly verbose for non-English examples, necessitating the division of the text into too small parts.

This behavior is undesirable for two primary reasons: i) it shatters the amount of information contained within each  
sub-unit processed by the model, potentially making it more challenging to understand long-term relations within the  
context; and ii) it escalates the computational cost of both training and inference, as it increases the number of tokens  
that need to be processed for the same text sample.

However, the inclusion of a new tokenizer in a pre-trained model poses a challenge, as there exists a direct mapping  
between the tokens used in pre-training and the model’s embedding representation. Merely replacing the tokenizer  
would break this mapping, likely resulting in odd model behavior and potentially requiring a considerable amount of  
additional pre-training to learn the new association pattern.

To address this issue, the approach taken in this work involves adapting the tokenizer to the new language while  
preserving the knowledge of the original language already embedded in the model. Inspired by the work of [\[11\], ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#7)this  
process involved three steps:

• Training a new tokenizer exclusively on Portuguese data sourced from Wikipedia. SentencePiece [\[12\] ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#7)imple-

mentation was used for this purpose, resulting in a tokenizer with 40,000 tokens.

Cabrita: closing the gap for foreign languages

PREPRINT

• Merging the original tokenizer with the newly created Portuguese tokenizer. During this merging process,

all tokens present in the original tokenizer were retained, and the new Portuguese tokens that were not yet  
represented in the vocabulary were appended until a total of 52,000 tokens were reached. The precedence  
level of each merge – BPE Score in the SentencePiece implementation – was maintained from both tokenizers,  
given that this led to a better token compression level.

• Resizing the model’s embedding and head matrix to accommodate the newly added tokens. The new rows

corresponding to the Portuguese tokens were appended to the end of the original matrix to ensure that the  
existing token mapping remained unaffected.

The result was a bilingual tokenizer, able to handle both English and Portuguese content efficiently.

2.2.2

Continuous pre-training

We use the Portuguese subset of the mC4 dataset [\[13\] ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#7)(hereafter called mC4-pt) as our pretraining corpus. Following  
the recipe in [\[1\], ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#7)we also apply quality filters based on MassiveText [\[14\] ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#7)to ensure our model is trained using high-  
quality documents.

First, we normalize each document independently using ftfy [\[15\]. ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#8)Then, we apply the quality filters. Unlike Mas-  
siveText, which only considers the stop words {the, be, to, of, and, that, have, with}, we use the Portuguese stop words  
from nltk [\[16\]; ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#8)we also keep only documents with at least 200 unique tokens, following the the procedure outlined  
in [\[1\]. ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#7)A document is kept in the dataset if it does not fall into any of the quality filters. Table [7 ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#9)shows the contribution  
of each filter to the final filtered dataset.

To estimate the total number of training tokens without processing the entire dataset, we assume that the remaining  
shards have similar sizes and behavior with respect to the quality filters. Based on this estimation, the unfiltered  
mC4-pt training dataset consists of approximately 169 million documents and 188 billion tokens, which reduces to  
133 million documents and 170 billion tokens after applying the low-quality filters. To convert these documents into  
training examples, we add <|bos|> and <|eos|> tokens to each document, and then pack these documents into  
sequences of 2048 tokens.

We perform the continuous pre-training step on TPUs using the EasyLM, which is a framework built in JAX/Flax and  
is a one-stop solution for training LLMs on TPU and GPU devices.

To perform continued pre-training in the Portuguese language, the original script and hyper-parameters of OpenL-  
LaMA training were employed. The model was initialized with the OpenLLaMA weights and then trained on an  
additional 7 billion tokens extracted from the Portuguese dataset.

The learning objective was the standard causal language modeling loss with the learning rate set to increase linearly  
from 0 to 3e-4 over 2,000 steps, followed by a cosine decrease to 3e-5 for the remaining 248,000 steps. The optimiza-  
tion algorithm used was AdamW, with a weight decay of 0.1, β1 set to 0.9, β2 set to 0.99, and a gradient clip value of  
1.0.

For training, a TPU v3-8 was utilized, with batches of 16, each containing a sequence of 2048 tokens. To achieve the  
target of 2048 samples in a batch, 128 accumulation steps were performed. This configuration resulted in a throughput  
of 7,900 tokens/second for the 3B model.

3

Evaluation

3.1

Tokenizer efficiency

For evaluating how alterations to the tokenizer affect text representation, a set of experiments were performed. These  
experiments involved the comparison of various tokenizer alternatives coming from different models and trained on  
distinct corpora. Figure [1 ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#4)presents a comparison of the token count required to represent 7400 words of the Constitu-  
tional law of the USA in both English and Portuguese (translated) for each of these tokenizer variations.

It can be noted that the standard OpenLLaMA implementation demonstrates highly inefficient behavior when applied  
to Portuguese data. It necessitates over 50% more tokens for representing the same text, in contrast to the multilingual  
Bloom and Portuguese pre-trained models (e.g. BERTimbau [\[17\], ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#8)PTT5 [\[18\], ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#8)Bertaú [\[19\]). ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#8)While certain other  
LLaMA-based implementations exhibit improved token counts, such as MPT [\[20\] ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#8)and Falcon [\[21\], ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#8)some inefficiency  
remains. This observation holds true even in comparison with chatGPT [\[22\], ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#8)which possesses a larger vocabulary than  
these LLaMA implementations.

PREPRINT

Figure 1: Tokenizer efficiency: the X axis show the number of tokens required to represent 7400 words of the Consti-  
tutional law of the USA in English, while the Y axis shows the same, but using a Portuguese translated version. The  
size of each sphere represents the vocabulary size of each tokenizer.

In contrast to these choices, the Cabrita tokenizer demonstrated the ability to enhance the OpenLLaMA token require-  
ments. It achieved a reduction of over 35% in the token requirements, bringing it in line with the token counts of the  
Bloom and native Portuguese implementations.

Furthermore, upon examining the token count in English, the Cabrita tokenizer even exhibited a slight improvement  
in the token count when compared with the original OpenLLaMA tokenizer, with no indication of degradation in this  
regard.

Ultimately, the Cabrita approach presents an excellent trade-off between Portuguese and English considerations, es-  
pecially when seeking models with comparable vocabulary sizes (52.000 tokens for Cabrita versus 250.680 tokens for  
Bloom).

3.2

Portuguese Benchmark results

To assess the efficacy of this proposal, 8 Portuguese evaluation datasets were employed across a variety of tasks:  
ASSIN 2 RTE and STS [\[23\], ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#8)FaQuAD [\[24\], ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#8)TweetSentBr [\[25\] ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#8)are inherently in Portuguese, while for AG News [\[26\], ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#8)IMDB [\[27\], ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#8)SST2 [\[28\] ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#8)and BoolQ [\[29\] ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#8)translated versions provided by the authors of the Sabiá series paper were  
utilized. Poeta’s benchmark [\[1\] ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#7)was not executed in our study due to the unavailability of its implementation at the  
time of our publication.

Table [1 ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#5)provides an overview of the datasets along with the specific few-shot configuration employed in each experi-  
ment.

A diverse array of tasks was carefully selected, spanning from binary and multi-class classification to Extractive  
Question Answering (QA). However, the absence of a comprehensive Portuguese benchmark prevented the utilization  
of a more extensive task set.

The Table [2 ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#5)exhibits the performance comparison of openCabrita3B with the base openLLaMA3B and a subsequent  
pre-training version that employs the openLLaMA tokenizer (referred to as openCabrita3BPTOnly).

The results are mixed but somewhat favoring openCabrita3B. When openCabrita3B performs better, it is notably supe-  
rior, as in ASSIN 2 RTE, TweetSentBr, and IMDB tasks. When openCabrita3BPTOnly outperforms, openCabrita3B  
is usually close, just a few scores behind. While ASSIN 2 STS is the only task where the original openLLaMA3b  
shows a better performance, which is unexpected but consistent with what was observed in other experiments [\[1\].](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#7)

parameter size compared to the other four options.

3.3

English Benchmark results

To assess the efficacy of this approach and demonstrate its bilingual capabilities, we conducted a series of evaluations  
using diverse English datasets, ensuring a comprehensive understanding of its performance. Table [4 ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#6)presents the  
performance of openCabrita in comparison with models trained mainly in English and without any fine-tuning for a  
specific language.

Despite a slight decrease in performance for English, the model’s capabilities remained robust and competitive across  
languages. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of different tokenizers—Open Llama and Cabrita—on the model’s  
output. Encouragingly, both tokenizers yielded highly consistent results, indicating that the introduction of new tokens  
had minimal impact on the model’s overall performance. This observation highlights the model’s resilience and  
suggests its versatility for diverse applications without significant trade-offs in performance.

4

Conclusion and next steps

This work is currently in progress and requires further development in terms of a more comprehensive set of models  
and experiments before arriving at any definitive conclusions. However, the outcomes obtained from modifying the  
tokenizer prior to performing continuous pre-training seem very promising.

Even in the absence of state-of-the-art performance enhancements, the openCabrita3b reaches a comparable metrics  
level when compared to the standard continuous pre-training approach while also improving inference time — an  
imperative factor in the context of deploying models for such applications that is commonly overlooked.

Looking ahead, the authors have outlined the following as their forthcoming initiatives:

• Test the same strategy in a more diverse set of base models

• Establish some type of benchmark and reperform runs for other models in order to have a comparison with

the same running methodology

5

Limitations

Scaling beyond 3B and for other languages Despite our best efforts, certain ranges of model sizes and experiments  
remain beyond our reach due to budget constraints. Consequently, our experimentation was limited to the Portuguese  
language and 3B size models.

 link to page 7 link to page 8 

Cabrita: closing the gap for foreign languages

PREPRINT

But, since the good results obtained, we are firmly convinced that employing larger-scale models could yield results at  
least as promising. This line of thinking could similarly be applied to other foreign languages, particularly considering  
the successful experiment with Chinese presented in [\[11\].](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#7)

Comparison to other base models and adapting strategies Due to the absence of a structured benchmark like  
Harness [\[30\] ](1793495606267-731924e1-c1fc-4fe0-9ce7-1e389f9df954-file150700.html#8)for the Portuguese language, our capacity to compare with other models and strategies for the same tasks  
is confined to the experiments we are able to perform. Consequently, the scope of comparisons we can undertake in  
this paper is restricted, both in terms of quantity and depth.
